abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) for audio typically benefits from larger pre-training corpora, but this relationship assumes that training data carries meaningful learning signal. In ocean acoustics, this assumption is often violated: passive recordings are dominated by waves, wind, and silence, with biological vocalizations occupying a small fraction of the total duration. We show that this overrepresentation of noise causes SSL models to allocate representational capacity to acoustically trivial structure, degrading downstream performance. Using BEATs as a testbed, we demonstrate that pre-training on 30 hours of salient recordings (segments containing animal vocalizations) outperforms 1,240 hours of unfiltered data on a 31-class marine mammal classification benchmark. Under linear probing, the manually curated salient set achieves markedly better accuracy than the full corpus, despite using 41 times less data. Automatic saliency-based filtering improves over unfiltered pre-training, but still falls well short of the manually curated salient set. Our findings suggest that, in domains where informative content is temporally sparse, data curation matters more than data scale for SSL pre-training.

oneSentenceThesis: 论文用 BEATs 做受控对比，说明在海洋被动录音中只保留含动物发声的 30 小时切带比 1240 小时未过滤录音在线性探测上高约 29 个百分点，而自动显著性过滤只能弥合很小一部分差距，原因是掩码预测按声学变化分配容量而非按生物相关性分配。
originalTitle: Drowning in Noise: On Signal Saliency in Self-Supervised Learning for Ocean Acoustics
